teaser: A stiff gentleman in a yellow coat offers a flower to a psychedelic whirlwind. In 1890.
review_notes:
Full title: Opus 217. Against the Enamel of a Background Rhythmic with Beats and Angles, Tones, and Tints, Portrait of M. Félix Fénéon in 1890.
Flower identified as a cyclamen (per MoMA).
Background pattern thought to derive from a Japanese print or kimono design (per MoMA); stated with 'probably'.
Fénéon's letter asking for an 'absolutely full-face' effigy, which Signac ignored: verify.
Fénéon: War Ministry clerk, arrested 1894, acquitted at the Trial of the Thirty; 'Novels in Three Lines' written for Le Matin in 1906.
Fénéon kept the portrait until his death in 1944; his reported coolness toward it is not stated in the lesson.
MoMA: gift of Mr. and Mrs. David Rockefeller.

lesson.text: Two pictures seem to have been glued together here. On the right, a man as stiff as a figure on a coin: strict profile, buttoned coat, top hat and cane. Behind him, a pinwheel of colors that would not look out of place on a 1960s rock poster. Paul Signac painted both, on purpose, in 1890.

The man is Félix Fénéon, 29 years old, the sharpest art critic in Paris. Four years earlier he had invented the name “Neo-Impressionism” for the painters who built pictures from small dots of pure color. Signac was one of them, and Fénéon was their best defender in print.

When Signac proposed a portrait, Fénéon is said to have asked for only one thing: to be shown full face. Signac did the opposite. He turned his friend sideways, like a profile on an old medal, and made the famous goatee the sharpest point in the picture.

lesson.title: The dandy
lesson.text: Start with the man himself, from the beard down to the hat.

spots.title: The profile
spots.text: Long nose, high forehead, a wisp of beard under the chin. Friends said Fénéon looked like Uncle Sam. Up close, the skin is made of orange, pink and green dots.

spots.title: The flower
spots.text: His fingers hold a white cyclamen by the stem, as delicately as a magician presenting a card. Its curling petals echo the swirl behind.

spots.title: Hat, gloves, cane
spots.text: The props of a dandy, a man who treats elegance as an art. The top hat is tipped so its yellow lining shows, a cool circle among all the curves.

lesson.text: The gesture is theatrical. Is he offering the flower to someone outside the frame, or conjuring the storm of color out of it? Signac never said. What we do know is where the background came from: probably the pattern of a Japanese print or kimono design, which Signac blew up to the size of a wall.

The painting's real title is a mouthful: “Opus 217. Against the Enamel of a Background Rhythmic with Beats and Angles, Tones, and Tints, Portrait of M. Félix Fénéon in 1890.” It is partly a joke on the scientific jargon the two friends loved.

“Opus” is the word composers use to number their works, and Signac numbered his paintings the same way. He thought of color as music. That long title promises rhythm, beats and angles, and the background delivers them. It is organized like a wheel.
The swirl has a hub. Watch the bands of pattern fan out from it.

lines.label: Toward the scrolls
lines.text: One edge shoots to the upper left, bordering a violet field with yellow curls.

lines.label: Toward the waves
lines.text: Another band slides down to the left, filled with zigzag ribbons of green, pink and red.

lines.label: Toward the leaves
lines.text: Below, an orange strip covered in white leaf shapes drops to the bottom edge.

lines.label: Toward the arcs
lines.text: To the right, stripes of yellow, violet and orange curve up and over Fénéon's head like a wave about to break.

lesson.text: Every band has its own pattern and its own pair of colors: yellow against violet, orange against blue, red against green. These are complementary colors, pairs that sit opposite each other on the color wheel and look most intense side by side. Signac had been drawing color diagrams for the scientist Charles Henry, and here he lets the diagram spin.
The portrait is a manifesto as much as a likeness: the critic who named Neo-Impressionism, standing in front of its theory of color turned into pure decoration.

Fénéon led a double life. By day he was a model clerk at the Ministry of War. He was also an anarchist, and in 1894 he was arrested and tried with 29 others on suspicion of links to bombings. He answered the judge with such wit that the jury acquitted him.

He could say more in fewer words than anyone. In 1906 he wrote hundreds of tiny news items for a Paris newspaper, each a complete drama in three lines, now published as “Novels in Three Lines”. The man in the yellow coat liked precision above all.
Fénéon kept this portrait for the rest of his life. He died in 1944. It later came to the Museum of Modern Art in New York as a gift of David Rockefeller and his wife.

spots.title: The target
spots.text: Concentric rings of orange, blue and cream. Stare at the middle and the bands seem to pulse, an optical effect Signac wanted.

spots.title: Yellow scrolls
spots.text: Curling shapes on violet, the most clearly Japanese part of the design.

spots.title: Floating discs
spots.text: Circles of yellow, green and striped orange drift on a purple band like planets.

spots.title: Stars
spots.text: Yellow stars on blue, tucked behind his elbow. With the stripes above, some viewers see a wink at the American flag and his Uncle Sam looks.

spots.title: Op. 217
spots.text: In the lower left corner, Signac's opus number, painted in dots like everything else.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: “P. Signac 90”, in blue on the starry band.

spots.title: Leaf pattern
spots.text: White leaves on orange, like wallpaper. It shows how flat the background is: no room, no depth, only surface.

quiz.question: Who was Félix Fénéon?
options: An art critic who named Neo-Impressionism
quiz.explanation: He was the critic who coined the term and defended the movement.

quiz.question: What does Fénéon hold out in his fingers?
quiz.explanation: He holds a white cyclamen by its stem.

quiz.question: Why does the title begin with “Opus 217”?
options: It was the 217th day of the year
It refers to a street address
Signac numbered his paintings like musical works
quiz.explanation: Signac borrowed the composer's word because he thought of color as music.

quiz.question: What are complementary colors?
options: Colors that are next to each other on the wheel
Pairs opposite each other on the color wheel
quiz.explanation: Opposite pairs such as yellow and violet look most intense side by side.

quiz.question: What happened to Fénéon in 1894?
options: He was tried as a suspected anarchist and acquitted
He became director of the Louvre
quiz.explanation: He was one of thirty defendants and the jury acquitted him.

facts.text: Signac showed Fénéon full face, as his friend had wished.
facts.explanation: Signac painted him in strict profile instead.

facts.text: The bands of the background fan out from a single hub.
facts.explanation: The patterned sections radiate from one point like a pinwheel.

facts.text: Fénéon sold the portrait as soon as it was finished.
facts.explanation: He kept it until his death in 1944.
